<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but PRO (B) left fewer of CON's live routes standing. CON's case rested on three pillars: the strikes spent monitoring, consumed an unexecuted threat, and left a movable stockpile. PRO answered each squarely: continuity of knowledge and camera coverage were already degraded before June (never rebutted by CON); the sites were originally found by intelligence, not inspectors; the "unspent threat" produced a climb from 20 to 60 percent and inspector obstruction, so it was leverage evaporating rather than conserved; and the stockpile without cascades or centrifuge manufacturing is a setback by definition. PRO's "window" reframe cleanly dissolved CON's "too dangerous to wait, too weak to fight" contradiction. CON's best material—the accounting-forces-a-parallel-program mechanism and PRO's honest admission it cannot locate the casks—was sharp and rhetorically memorable, but CON's closing largely repeated "the signal was already working" without engaging PRO's point that the signal was demonstrably failing at each step. Both sides suffered clipped turns (PRO twice, CON once), a minor execution cost that does not change the outcome.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing turn on "a threat executed is a threat consumed": by showing the unexecuted threat coincided with Iran's escalation to 60 percent, camera removal, and breach findings, PRO converted CON's central slogan into evidence that the deterrent was already hollow, and CON's final speech did not answer it.</best_rebuttal>
